newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY NEEDS CONSENSUS TO SLASH INFLATION - OFFICIAL.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY NEEDS CONSENSUS TO SLASH INFLATION - OFFICIAL.

text.p: Hungary could push inflation down below 10 percent in 1998 if the government reaches a satisfactory prices and wages agreement with employers and unions, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Tuesday.
"From a pure economic sense this is possible," Deputy Secretary of State Tamas Tetenyi told Reuters.
But Tetenyi said such conditions depended on a determination from all sections of society to resist inflationary pressures.

Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told the daily Magyar Hirlap on Monday that Hungary, urged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to cut its inflation more quickly, may revise its 1998 economic policy plans.
According to the original government plans, Hungary should reduce inflation to 16 to 18 percent in 1997 from 23.6 percent in 1996 and cut it by a further five percentage points in 1998.

Medgyessy, following talks last weekend with a senior IMF official at the World Economic Forum in Davos, said that Hungary may prepare alternative 1998 budget drafts, with one of them including a larger inflation cut than previously planned.
Tetenyi said economic factors do not justify that inflation should remain as high as 13 percent in 1998. The figure could drop to eight to nine percent next year, he said.

But the past few years' economic figures caused higher inflation expectations than government forecasts, resulting in larger wage claims and price rises than necessary, he added. This was an important factor which itself could limit the pace of reduction in inflation.
"While these social behaviour patterns exist, a dramatic fall in inflation, for example from 18 percent to eight percent, cannot happen," he said.
"The condition (of single-digit inflation in 1998) comes from a social-political will (to keep inflation down) which should appear in all price and wage bargaining," Tetenyi added.
Tetenyi declined to predict the chances of such a wide social consensus on wages and prices ahead of the 1998 elections, which if anything are expected to add to upward pressure on wages and prices.
A monthly Reuters poll in January showed that analysts expected inflation to drop to around 18.5 percent in 1997 and 15.75 percent in 1998.
